🧱 One controlCheckBox { name: "showPlot"; label: qsTr("Show plot") }
type · name (for R, later) · label (what users see)
☑️ CheckBoxCheckBox { name: "x"; label: qsTr("…"); checked: true }
✏️ TextFieldTextField { name: "x"; label: qsTr("…"); defaultValue: "999" }
🔢 IntegerField / DoubleFieldIntegerField { name: "x"; label: qsTr("…"); defaultValue: 2; min: 0; max: 10 }

🗂️ GroupGroup { title: qsTr("…") …controls… } · a titled box
📂 SectionSection { title: qsTr("…") …controls… } · folded away
🪆 NestingPut a control inside a CheckBox’s { } → it’s greyed out until the box is ticked
⚠️ Three rulesTypes start with a Capital · text goes in "quotes" · every { needs its }

Get the module & a GitHub token ⏱ 5 min 0:20–0:25

🌐 Browser Grab the module

Download the starter module and unzip it somewhere you’ll find again (e.g. your Documents folder).

⬇️ Download jaspDataWrangling.zip

🐙 GitHub Create a token

Logged in to GitHub? Open https://github.com/settings/tokens/new and fill in:

NoteJASP
Expiration90 days
Scopes☐ tick nothing!
ThenGenerate token ↓
🤔 Why a token at all?

Our module downloads two packages (jaspBase, jaspGraphs) from GitHub. Without a login, GitHub allows only 60 requests per hour per network, and the whole room shares one network. A token gives each of you your own allowance. With no boxes ticked, it can only read public stuff, so it can't do any harm.

Copy it now!

GitHub shows the token (ghp_...) only once. Lost it? No drama: just make a new one.

📊 RStudio Hand the token to R

Open RStudio (just RStudio, not the project yet) and run in the Console:

file.edit("~/.Renviron")

Add this line with your own token, press Enter once (R can skip a last line without a line break 🙃), and save:

GITHUB_PAT=ghp_paste-your-token-here
🤔 Why this file?

.Renviron is read every time R starts, so you only do this once on this computer. R picks it up in the next R session, which starts automatically when you open the project.

Install the module ⏱ 20 min 0:25–0:45

📁 Finder / Explorer Open the project

Double-click jaspDataWrangling.Rproj. RStudio’s Console should greet you with:

- Project '~/.../jaspDataWrangling' loaded. [renv 1.x.x]
😵 No such line?

RStudio didn't open it as a project. Use File → Open Project… and pick the .Rproj file.

📊 RStudio Did the token arrive?

Sys.getenv("GITHUB_PAT")

It should print something starting with ghp_.

😵 It prints an empty ""

R hasn't read your .Renviron yet. Session → Restart R, then try again.

📊 RStudio Install everything

renv::install(".")

Sit back ☕ This compiles a few packages and takes a while. You’re done when R says Successfully installed.

😵 Red ERROR somewhere?

Scroll up to the first red ERROR: that's the real cause. dependency 'X' is not available only means X failed earlier. Screenshot that first error and wave at Leo 👋

Load the module in JASP ⏱ 10 min 0:45–0:55

🧮 JASP Open the developer settings

Menu (☰, top left) → Preferences → Advanced. Find the Development module box and keep this window open.

📊 RStudio Find where renv put everything

With the project still open, run:

.libPaths()

Copy the first path, the one marked [1]. It contains jaspDataWrangling and ends with your R version and computer type, something like:

[1] "/Users/you/.../jaspDataWrangling-5f03db05/macos/R-4.5/aarch64-apple-darwin20"

Copy only the path itself: no [1], no quotes.

🧮 JASP Paste it

Under Development module: tick Enable renv mode, paste the path into Project library, and type jaspDataWrangling as Module name.

🧮 JASP Lift-off!

Click Install Developer Module. A Data Wrangling button appears on the ribbon 🎉 Open Control Playground and poke every control: watch the text, table and plot react. Then peek at Missing Values: that’s the one you’ll build.

How a JASP module works ⏱ 15 min 0:55–1:10

You just played with Control Playground. Time to open the hood! A JASP module is an R package with a few extra files for the JASP interface. Every analysis is made of three pieces:

📋
Description.qmlMenu entryPuts “Control Playground” in the ribbon
→
🎛️
controlPlayground.qmlControlsThe left panel you clicked
→
📊
controlPlayground.RComputationThe text, table & plot on the right
📂 What’s in the box? Click any file or folder
👈 Pick a file to find out what it does.

today later don’t touch

📋 Start with the menu

The easiest piece to see: inst/Description.qml decides what appears when you click Data Wrangling on the ribbon. Open it and compare it with the menu in JASP:

GroupTitle
{
    title: qsTr("Playground")              // a heading in the menu
}

Analysis
{
    title: qsTr("Control Playground")      // an item you can click
    func : "controlPlayground"             // the R function it runs
    qml  : "controlPlayground.qml"         // the window it opens
}

Your first edit: add a heading of your own to the Data Wrangling menu. Any title you like! No code given this time: the snippet above has everything you need.

When you’re done: save → in RStudio’s Console run renv::install(".") → in JASP, Install Developer Module again → click Data Wrangling.

💡 Hint 1

How did the heading “Playground” get into the menu? Find that word in Description.qml.

💡 Hint 2

You need a new block of the same type as the one around “Playground”. Copy it, change one thing. Where you paste it decides where it appears.

🔓 Still stuck? Show the answer
GroupTitle
{
    title: qsTr("My corner")
}

Paste it just above the last } of the file, so it lands at the bottom of the menu.

👯 Pair up: QML detectives

Work with your neighbour: one of you opens the QML file, the other opens JASP. Then solve these missions together, switching roles whenever you like:

🕵️Code📊 RStudio · inst/qml/controlPlayground.qml
⇄
🧭JASP🧮 Control Playground

Round 1 · Spot it 🔍

Just look, no editing yet.

Round 2 · Change it ✏️

For each mission: predict first, then edit. Make all four edits, then reinstall once (renv::install(".")) and check your predictions in JASP.

🔍 Reveal the answers (after you've tried!)

Round 1. info is the help text behind the ⓘ button. Ticked at start: “Show histogram”, “Teal” and “Show what R received”, each with checked: true. “Mark the mean” sits inside the “Show histogram” CheckBox, so it follows its parent. The drawer is a Section.
Round 2. The name box gets wider. JASP won’t accept 20000 because of max: 10000: raise it to e.g. max: 50000. With decimals: 2 the slider shows 1.25 instead of 1.2. And your number appears at the end of the dropdown list (mind the quotes and commas!).

Try it: read the QML, predict the window 🎮

Add your first button ⏱ 15 min 1:10–1:25


Time to build in your own window: Missing Values. Open inst/qml/missingValues.qml, look at each target picture, and rebuild it. Work in pairs, start with ⭐, and go as far as you like. It only has to look right: making it actually work is Session 3!

⭐ A first question











The Calm Minds team opens their data file and asks the obvious question: “How much of this is missing?” Before any numbers, they need a way to ask for them.


Build this:

⭐⭐ Missing isn’t always empty











Plot twist: the team didn’t only leave cells empty. Some research assistants typed 999, others -99, whenever a participant skipped a question. A good tool lets users decide what counts as missing, and how to sort the report… but these settings only matter once someone actually asks for the report.

Bonus: more controls to play with 🧰 Optional · for fast finishers


Checkboxes are just the start. Control Playground uses a whole toolbox of controls; here they are, one by one. Every mini control below is clickable, so try them!


✏️TextField
Free text, like a name or a title.
Show the QML
TextField
{
    name        : "yourName"
    label       : qsTr("Your name")
    defaultValue: "JASP"
}
🔢IntegerField
Whole numbers only, with limits.
Show the QML
IntegerField
{
    name        : "sampleSize"
    label       : qsTr("Sample size")
    defaultValue: 100
    min         : 2
    max         : 10000
}
🎯DoubleField
Numbers with decimals (and minus signs, if you allow them).
Show the QML
DoubleField
{
    name          : "mean"
    label         : qsTr("Mean")
    defaultValue  : 0
    negativeValues: true
}
🎚️Slider
Drag to pick a value in a range.
Show the QML
Slider
{
    name    : "sd"
    label   : qsTr("Standard deviation")
    value   : 1
    min     : 0.1
    max     : 5
    decimals: 1
}
🔽DropDown
Pick one option from a list.
Show the QML
DropDown
{
    name  : "seed"
    label : qsTr("Random seed")
    values: ["42", "2026", "123"]
}
🔘RadioButtonGroup
Exactly one of a few choices, all visible at once.
Bar colour
Show the QML
RadioButtonGroup
{
    name : "barColor"
    title: qsTr("Bar colour")
    RadioButton { value: "teal";   label: qsTr("Teal"); checked: true }
    RadioButton { value: "orange"; label: qsTr("Orange") }
    RadioButton { value: "purple"; label: qsTr("Purple") }
}
🗂️Group
A titled box that keeps related controls together.
Simulate data
Show the QML
Group
{
    title: qsTr("Simulate data")

    IntegerField { name: "sampleSize"; label: qsTr("Sample size") }
    DoubleField  { name: "mean";       label: qsTr("Mean") }
}
📂Section
A fold-out area for extra options, closed by default.
Behind the scenes
Show the QML
Section
{
    title: qsTr("Behind the scenes")

    CheckBox { name: "showOptions"; label: qsTr("Show what R received") }
}


How to try one for real: copy a snippet into inst/qml/missingValues.qml (inside the Form { }), save, run renv::install("."), and refresh JASP. All of them live in inst/qml/controlPlayground.qml too, if you want to see them in context.


🧩 Mini challenge: tweak the Slider
Make the Slider run from 0 to 100, start at 50, and show no decimals. Which three lines do you change? (Answer: min, max and value, plus decimals: 0.)
